newsitem.title: USA: Hartford seen growing under new chairman.
newsitem.headline: Hartford seen growing under new chairman.

text.p: Diversified insurance company The Hartford is likely to pursue its growth plans more aggressively under new chairman Ramani Ayer, analysts said on Monday.
Ayer, 49, took over as chairman, president and chief executive officer on Feb 1, following the retirement of Don Frahm.
Ayer is only the ninth chairman in the company's 187-year history. He had been president and chief operating officer of worldwide property-casualty operations since 1991.
"He's a little more interested in being active and making his mark in the world, so The Hartford might be a little more aggressive this year," said Gary Ransom, analyst at Conning & Co.
"He's viewed favorably," said Pete Wade, vice president at Lehman Bros.

"People view Ramani as an extremely competent manager and strategist in the insurance business, and in many respects largely credit him with the strength of some of The Hartford's various franchises - such as their overall property-casualty operation, and the distribution strategy that they have."
The Hartford said earlier on Monday that its fourth quarter 1996 core earnings grew by 59 percent to $1.65 per share.
Most Wall Street analysts were expecting growth of 46 percent to $1.52, according to First Call, which monitors analysts' projections.
The Hartford cited improved underwriting performance in workers' compensation and personal automobile insurance.
It also cited an 11 percent improvement in core earnings for all segments of the life operations, with particularly strong results in individual annuities.
The Hartford's stock was up 0-3/8 to 73-3/4 at 1535 EST.

Analysts said the stock was traditionally under-valued, considering the strength of The Hartford's life business and its exclusive arrangement to write business for the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP).
"Not enough people on Wall Street know the management, or know the story or know the strength of the franchise. Because if they did, the stock would be trading at more than 73-3/8," said Wade.
However, Wade said that analysts were disappointed that The Hartford's personal lines business grew by only 1.3 percent in the fourth quarter and 2.8 percent for the year.
He said the company was capable of much better figures, given its built-in competitive advantage with AARP and its distribution network.
